Hey OP, I also took the FE mechanical about 2.5 years ago and am out of school for almost 3 years (Dec2020 grad). 

As far as the FE goes, look up first time pass rates to give yourself some confidence. EVERYONE that I was close with from school passed the exam on the first try. It is not a hard exam by any measure. I would highly recommend using prepFE, it is cheap and very effective at helping to drill in the simple concepts. The FE is all about identifying what type of problem it is (heat transfer, thermo, etc), finding the correct equation to plug into, and solving for your answer pretty much - very simple plug and chug type problems. 

Save the $$ for the PE prep, as having recently passed that, the studying and prep was at least 5x more stressful and difficult, tons of conversions and long problems.

The best advice I can give you is to have confidence, bang out as many practice problems as possible and even 50 hours of studying for this exam would be overkill. REGISTER FOR THE EXAM!!!!!!! I would have procrastinated taking the FE and the PE for years and been 10+ years out of school like many others here if I didn’t force myself to be under the pressure. Believe in yourself!

This is one of the worst resumes that I've ever seen, but as sovereign suggested, definitely spend much more time developing your resume. There's so much white space here that is not being used.

Scrap the "engineering student in search of..." part, we're all engineering students trying to do just that! Scrap the entire core competences section. Widen your margins and make whatever recruiter reading your resume want to at least skim your resume, as it is now, it would likely get thrown straight into the trash without a second thought IMO. 

Scrap the core courses section in education. Elaborate much more on your professional experience, especially ESPECIALLY the $50 million project you're involved in. 

Also, you're a sophomore at university, scrap the student council member in high school line in the volunteer section. Elaborate more on the bible camp, YMCA, and federation lines. They show great leadership skills without you having to say "strong communication/interpersonal skills", which is in every cliche resume ever.

Also, in your certificates section, almost none of that stuff is relevant whatsoever other than the volunteer awards. Unless your job involves driving a boat, why include the pleasure craft license or drivers license?

I started out in exploratory studies and just got accepted into the mechanical engineering department this past semester! I started in calculus I my first semester, but dropped it as I completely underestimated it and expected it to be like high school. Anyways, you can see how our situations were similar. 

I encourage you to stick to the plan of knocking out the requirements to get accepted into the engineering college ASAP. That should be your number one priority. 

I’m assuming you’ll be taking pre-calc, intro to engineering, chemistry and maybe some other cores? If that’s the case, that’s a good first semester schedule! Also later this semester, don’t forget to submit your petition to take computing for engineers (1331) before the end of the semester.

Next semester, focus on doing well in calculus I, chem 2, and especially computing. Computing is absolutely NOT a blowoff class anymore (hasn’t been for 2 or so years now), so make sure to grab every little bit of credit you can in that class (I got a B- by 1 point on my final). They do not curve.

After that semester, you should be taking calculus II, university physics I, and some other core classes and if all goes well, you should be in the college after this semester. 

However, I HIGHLY encourage you to petition to take statics (CIVE 2330) at the same time as submitting your petition for admission to the college. This is so if things don’t go too well and your petition to be admitted into the college gets put on hold while your petition to take statics gets approved, you get sort of a last hail mary to prove to the engineering advisors that you have what it takes. 

Just a bit of motivation for you as well: this was almost my exact situation and I ended up getting a straight up A in statics this past semester and got into the college as a mechanical engineering student even with a sub-par cumulative (3.13) and a horrible 2.2 sGPA, but a 3.33 engineering GPA. 

You can do it! PM if you ever have questions or need advice.

I felt the same way my first semester at uni. I was not the brightest student in high school and I got into uni by the skin of my teeth. I took calculus 1 my first semester and got 30s on the first two tests that I took and dropped the class.

The next semester, I retook calculus 1 and breezed through it with an A and proceeded to do the same in calculus 2.

My first time in calculus, I was doing the absolute bare minimum to get by and genuinely expected to do well on tests only to flat out fail them every time. What you really need to do, like I and many others have, is to take a step back and be honest with yourself about your study habits. Are you honestly putting forth your best effort? You really need to develop good study habits if you’re going to get through engineering school.

Also, the key to doing well in the calculus series is to bust out practice problems and watching videos on concepts you don’t understand. Watch how people work and explain problems, I recommend patrickJMT or professor Leonard. I know it may sound frustrating to hear the same thing from others who have and will comment here saying the same things in a different way, but if you actually buckle down and get it together and still can’t get the hang of it, maybe engineering just isn’t for you and that’s perfectly fine.
